name: zint
desc: Barcode encoding library supporting over 50 symbologies
why: Encodes over fifty barcode symbologies, a broad and oddly fascinating transform of data into printed patterns, though still a library.

brief.what_it_is: Zint is an open source barcode generator. It takes data plus a chosen symbology and produces a printable barcode image. The README describes it as a suite of programs plus an encoding library: a Qt-based GUI (Zint Barcode Studio), a CLI executable named zint, and a library (libzint) for embedding in other software. Output can be saved as BMP, EMF, EPS, GIF, PCX, PNG, SVG or TIF. The supported list covers roughly 90 named formats, including linear codes like Code 128 and EAN-13, postal codes like Royal Mail 4-State and USPS Intelligent Mail, and 2D codes like QR Code, Data Matrix, PDF417, Aztec and MaxiCode.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Zint exists to allow easy encoding of data in the wide range of public domain barcode standards, and to allow that capability to be integrated into your own programs.
brief.install_notes: Neither the homepage nor the README gave install steps or a sample command line. The homepage says the manual covers compiling, running and using Zint, and the README says docs are in docs/manual.txt or docs/manual.html, also online at zint.org.uk/manual. Ports exist in other languages (OkapiBarcode in Java, Pascal, C#, Barcode.new), and gLabels includes Zint support.
brief.standout: Breadth is the main draw: one open library covering dozens of obscure postal, pharmaceutical and industrial symbologies alongside the common ones. It ships as a GUI, a CLI and a C library from a single codebase, and the library is BSD-3 licensed while the CLI and GUI are GPL.
brief.status: Unknown from the pages I read. The GitHub README copyright line says 2026, the homepage lists current-looking features (rMQR, Mailmark, Zint Barcode Studio), and the project says it is mirrored on GitHub and hosted on SourceForge. I did not find a release date or last-commit date.
brief.caveats: Support is volunteer-run and the README says answers may take up to a week. The maintainers say they cannot support use with commercial packages such as MS Office or Crystal Reports. Licensing is split: the library is BSD-3, but the GUI and CLI are GPLv3 or later, and historical versions before 2.5 are GPL. The homepage's own FAQ is vague about cost, saying only that the project is open source. The scout note calls it 'still a library', but the README describes CLI and GUI programs as well, so the tool is more than a library.
quotes: Zint is a suite of programs to allow easy encoding of data in any of the wide range of public domain barcode standards and to allow integration of this capability into your own programs.
Automate barcode generation from the command line for scripts and workflows.
Please remember that Zint is developed by volunteers.

judge.reason: Zint’s broad support for obscure postal and industrial barcode formats makes a mundane data-to-pattern transform unexpectedly worth exploring.

entry.title: zint
entry.tldr: A barcode generator that turns text into around ninety symbologies, from QR codes and Data Matrix to postal codes with bars of different heights.
entry.deeper_look:
Zint is a suite of programs for encoding data as barcodes. The Homebrew formula installs the command-line program, `zint`. It takes your data and a chosen symbology and writes an image file. The README lists BMP, EMF, EPS, GIF, PCX, PNG, SVG and TIF as output formats. The same codebase also produces a Qt-based GUI called Zint Barcode Studio and a C library, libzint, for embedding in other software.

The interest is in the range. Beyond the barcodes on a cereal box (Code 128, EAN-13), the list includes postal codes such as Royal Mail 4-State and USPS Intelligent Mail, and 2D codes such as QR Code, Data Matrix, PDF417, Aztec and MaxiCode. Each one is a different answer to the same question: how do you pack data into a printed pattern that a cheap scanner can read despite smudges, skew and bad printing?

The project's stated aim is "easy encoding of data in any of the wide range of public domain barcode standards" and to let you integrate that into your own programs. Trying several symbologies on the same string shows how differently each one spends its space.
